prop3-naboths-vineyard-when-the-process-.reason: Story first; the answer (Yahweh names the substance and ignores the wrapper) arrives mid-lesson, and the test for today's forms is only stated in the final paragraph.
prop3-naboths-vineyard-when-the-process-.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. How can paperwork be perfect and still be wrong? When every lawful step is doing the work that a threat or a sword would otherwise do. Ahab's court had a fast, an assembly, two witnesses and a verdict, and Yahweh still called it killing and taking (1 Kings 21:19). He judges the substance, not the wrapper. Here is how the account exposes it.
prop3-naboths-vineyard-when-the-process-.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. How does Ahab's court case expose the forms that carry injustice? Every step looked lawful, and Yahweh ignored the minutes and named what was done: a man killed and his vineyard taken. So the question for any property business is not only "is this legal?" It is whether a lawful step is doing the work a threat would do: a fee timed to trap, a notice served when it cannot be answered, a clause written to be misread. When the form carries the violence, the form is the evidence.

teen.open: Can something follow every rule and still be wrong? Yes. King Ahab used a real court and real witnesses to take a man's vineyard, and Yahweh called it murder.
teen.close: So the answer is that Yahweh looks at what really happened, not at how neat the paperwork was. If the rules are being used to hurt someone, the rules do not make it right.

senior.open: The title says the paperwork was perfect and it was still wrong. Ahab's court followed every recognizable form, and Yahweh set it all aside to ask, "Hast thou killed, and also taken possession?" (1 Kings 21:19).
senior.close: So the answer is that a lawful process does not sanctify an unjust act. The right test asks whether a lawful step is doing what a threat would otherwise do, and where it is, the form is not a defence but the evidence.

prop2-the-landmark-is-a-moral-object.reason: Opens on the commandment and asks why; who moves the line (the neighbour on his own land, unseen, toward the weak) is built up across the middle, and today's form arrives at the end.
prop2-the-landmark-is-a-moral-object.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Who moves the line when no one is watching? The neighbour standing on his own land, quietly, so that nothing looks stolen. Boundary theft leaves no evidence, which is why Yahweh gave it its own commandment (Deuteronomy 19:14). It travels toward the fatherless, who cannot fight back, and Yahweh says their Redeemer is mighty (Proverbs 23:10-11). Here is how the Word names it.
prop2-the-landmark-is-a-moral-object.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Who moves the line when no one is watching? Anyone who quietly restates a boundary in his own favour, against someone who will not read closely. Yahweh saw that this theft hides itself, so He named it, warned that it targets the weak, and said the office of a prince makes it worse (Hosea 5:10). Today the landmark is the survey, the lease, the fee schedule and the notice period. Know where the real line is, and leave it where the fathers set it.

teen.open: Who moves a property line when nobody is looking? Usually the neighbour next door, a little at a time, so it never looks like stealing.
teen.close: So the answer is that quiet stealing is still stealing. Today the line is often on paper, like a lease. Know where the real line is, and do not move it.

senior.open: The title asks who moves the boundary when no one watches. The Word answers that it is the neighbour on his own ground, by a theft that leaves no evidence, which is why Yahweh gave landmarks their own commandment (Deuteronomy 19:14).
senior.close: So the answer is that the quiet encroacher is the offender Yahweh named, and his likeliest victim is the one who cannot afford to fight. In our day the landmark is written: the survey, the lease, the fee schedule. Leave it where it was set.

prop4-a-sale-was-a-lease-of-years.reason: Answers early ('So what did a buyer actually buy? THE HARVESTS'), but ends on the redemption clause and a list of practices rather than landing harvests-priced-by-years.
prop4-a-sale-was-a-lease-of-years.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Are you buying the land or just its harvests? Under Leviticus 25 a buyer bought the harvests, never the ground, because every fiftieth year the land went back to its family. So the price was set by counting the years of harvest left until the jubilee. Here is how Yahweh wrote that pricing method down.
prop4-a-sale-was-a-lease-of-years.example: SAME FIELD, DIFFERENT YEARS. Say a field yields a harvest each year. Bought with thirty years left before the jubilee, the buyer is paying for thirty harvests, so the price is high. Bought with five years left, he is paying for five, so the price is low. Same field, same soil, and the price moves only with the count of harvests remaining (Leviticus 25:16). Seller and buyer count the same years by the same rule, so neither one is guessing.
prop4-a-sale-was-a-lease-of-years.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Are you buying the land or just its harvests? In Israel, only the harvests, priced by the number of years left, the same way for buyer and seller. The land itself belonged to Yahweh and returned to its family. That is still the honest way to see an income property: it is worth its remaining years of real income, and a price that floats above that is a wager. Price by the years, tell both sides the same count, and keep a way back open for the brother who fell behind.

teen.open: When someone in Israel bought a field, what did they really get? Not the land forever. They bought the harvests until the year of jubilee.
teen.close: So the answer is the harvests. The price depended on how many harvest years were left, and both sides counted the same way. That kept the price honest.

senior.close: So the answer is that the buyer purchased harvests, not ground. The price rose and fell with the years remaining before the jubilee, counted by one rule for both parties. An income property is still worth its remaining years of income, and pricing beyond that is a wager.

prop1-the-land-is-his-and-it-was-given-b.reason: Opens on land given by name; the answer to who holds the deed (Leviticus 25:23, 'the land is mine') comes only in the second half, though the final sentence lands it well.
prop1-the-land-is-his-and-it-was-given-b.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Who really holds the deed? Yahweh does. He gave land to families by name, on purpose, and He kept the title: "the land is mine; for ye are strangers and sojourners with me" (Leviticus 25:23). We hold the use, and we owe Him an account for it. Here is how the Word shows both halves.
prop1-the-land-is-his-and-it-was-given-b.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Who really holds the deed? Yahweh holds the title, and you hold the use. He gave ground to families by name, so owning land is not worldly. He kept the title, so owning land is not a license to do as you please. Stewardship is ownership with an Owner. That is why a boundary, a price, a tenant and a building plan all carry moral weight in this course: the One who made the ground handed you the use of it.

teen.open: Who really owns your land? Yahweh does. He gives families the use of it, but He keeps the title.
teen.close: So the answer is that the land is His, and we take care of it for Him. That means owning things is good, and it also means we answer to Him for how we use them.

senior.open: The title asks who truly holds the deed. Leviticus 25:23 settles it: the land is Yahweh's, and the holder is a stranger and sojourner with Him, even while the land is given to families by name.
senior.close: So the answer is that Yahweh keeps the title and grants the use. That cuts against both absolute dominion and the false piety that despises ownership. Stewardship is ownership with an Owner, and every decision about the ground is made as one who will give account.

prop6-the-field-before-the-house.reason: Opens on Proverbs 24:27 with the producing field first and names what happens to a property bought on hope; ends on the order as the difference between a holding that feeds a family and a mocked foundation.

prop5-the-deed-the-witnesses-and-the-ear.reason: The answer (hope: houses and fields shall be possessed again, Jeremiah 32:15) is in the middle; the lesson ends on a records-keeping standard, not on why Jeremiah sealed it.
prop5-the-deed-the-witnesses-and-the-ear.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Why would Jeremiah seal a deed for a field he would never plow? Because Yahweh promised that "Houses and fields and vineyards shall be possessed again in this land" (Jeremiah 32:15). The careful deed, the witnesses and the clay jar were not caution. They were hope, a legible claim left for a family who would one day come home. Here is how the Word shows it.
prop5-the-deed-the-witnesses-and-the-ear.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Why would Jeremiah seal a deed for a field he would never plow? Because he believed Yahweh. With the army at the walls, he signed, sealed, took witnesses, weighed the silver, and stored the deed in clay to last many days, so a grandchild could prove the claim in a land restored. The paperwork was the faith. Your records can carry the same hope: a named keeper, a working copy and a kept copy, witnessed, and meant to last for generations.

teen.open: Why would anyone buy a field right before an army takes the city? Jeremiah did, because Yahweh promised the land would be lived in again.
teen.close: So the answer is hope. Jeremiah kept the deed safe in a clay jar so his family could claim the field later. Good records can be a way of trusting Yahweh's promise.

senior.open: The title asks why Jeremiah took such care over a deed for a field he would never work. The next verse gives the reason: Yahweh promised that houses, fields and vineyards would be possessed again in the land (Jeremiah 32:15).
senior.close: So the answer is that the deed was an act of hope, not mere prudence. Signed, sealed, witnessed and stored for many days, it was a claim left for a family's return, and a household's records can still be kept in that same faith.

prop7-the-tenant-is-a-neighbour-and-the-.reason: Answers in the first lines (Leviticus 19:13, before sunrise), but closes on the tenant-as-neighbour ceiling rather than landing what the before-sunrise clock asks of the business.
prop7-the-tenant-is-a-neighbour-and-the-.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Is the payday really due tonight? Yes. Yahweh set the clock before sunrise, because the worker is poor and has set his heart on that money (Deuteronomy 24:15), and his cry reaches the Lord of armies (James 5:4). For a property business that means the crew and the tradesman are paid on terms with no float taken from them, deposits go back on time with every deduction shown, and a late fee never becomes profit. The one least able to wait must not be made to wait.

teen.open: When does Yahweh say a worker should be paid? The same day, before the sun goes down.
teen.close: So yes, the pay is due tonight. The worker is counting on it for food. Paying on time is how you treat him like a neighbour.

senior.open: The title asks whether a worker's pay is truly due the same day. Leviticus 19:13 says the wage shall not stay with the employer all night until the morning.
senior.close: So the answer is yes. The duty is measured by the worker's need rather than the payer's convenience, and in a property business it reaches the tradesman's pay, the tenant's deposit, and any fee that has begun to feed on the person least able to bear it.

prop8-handed-forward-or-handed-to-a-fool.reason: Opens on Proverbs 13:22 and Solomon's fear; the answer (only if both a prepared position and a formed successor are handed on purpose) comes in David's two halves and the double-entry standard late.
prop8-handed-forward-or-handed-to-a-fool.open: THE QUESTION IN THE TITLE. Will your grandchildren inherit wisdom along with the property? Only if you hand it to them on purpose. The asset transfers either way; competence and conviction do not. Solomon feared leaving his work to a fool (Ecclesiastes 2:18-19). David answered with two halves: he prepared everything for his son, and he charged him out loud to trust Yahweh, whom he himself had known. Here is how the Word shows it.
prop8-handed-forward-or-handed-to-a-fool.close: BACK TO THE QUESTION. Will your grandchildren inherit wisdom along with the property? They will if you do what David did. Prepare the position: documents found, a keeper named, real numbers, boundaries known, tradesmen paid. Then form the successor: teach these principles early and before the transfer, and hand over your own tested trust in Yahweh. One half alone hands a stranger a bill or a believer a mess. Both halves together reach the grandchildren, in hands that already know whose ground it is.

teen.open: Will your family's house come with the wisdom to run it? Not by itself. Things pass down automatically, but wisdom has to be taught on purpose.
teen.close: So the answer is to do both. Get things in order, and teach the next generation early who the land really belongs to, so they are ready when it is theirs.

senior.open: The title asks whether wisdom will pass down with the property. Solomon himself feared it would not (Ecclesiastes 2:18-19), and the asset transfers whether the heir is wise or a fool.
senior.close: So the answer is that wisdom passes only when it is handed on deliberately. David prepared the position and charged his son before the assembly. Both halves, an ordered estate and a formed successor, are needed for an inheritance to reach the children's children.
